verified_closed.prior_finding: CRITICAL — /api/v1/users/{userID}/* has no authn/authz; userID comes from the URL (IDOR, full cross-tenant read/write)
verified_closed.evidence: Decision 6 + Task 6 move userID to session context and put RequireAuth+RequireAccess on the prefix. Independently verified in code: service.CreateChatInput (costing.go:164-166) has only Title; OrderInput (costing.go:87-99), UserSettings (:77-85) and MarketFeedbackInput (deepseek.go:17-29) carry no owner field; UserID exists only on output types CalculationResult (:114) and Chat (:154); decodeJSON sets DisallowUnknownFields (http.go:230) and is used by all four decode sites (http.go:74, 99, 142, 194); repository queries are scoped by user_id (postgres.go:183, 258, 282, 306, 410, 431). handleDeleteChat reads only the `hard` query param. With the path segment gone there is no remaining owner channel.

verified_closed.prior_finding: HIGH — POST /auth/yandex accepts a caller-supplied OAuth access token and mints a session
verified_closed.evidence: Decision 7 removes the route, HandleYandexLogin (auth.go:42-97), persistYandexToken (yandexAuth.js:61-79) and the implicit branch in AuthCallback.jsx:36-45. Acceptance criterion and post-deploy check assert 404. Residual: the nginx `location = /auth/yandex` blocks in client/nginx.conf and in the deploy.yml heredoc become dead config — harmless, worth removing in Task 9.

verified_closed.prior_finding: HIGH — anonymous row injection into `users` could pre-create rows carrying access columns
verified_closed.evidence: Decision 13 keeps userModel ID-only (postgres.go:15-22) and upsertUser uses OnConflict DoNothing with userModel{ID} (postgres.go:550-555), so the anonymous path cannot write role/has_access; the columns take their DEFAULTs ('user'/FALSE). EnsureUser restricts the ON CONFLICT update list to email/display_name. No API path writes role.

findings.location: tech-spec.md — Data Models, migration 004_access_control.up.sql (INSERT ... VALUES ('ADMIN_LOGIN_2','admin',TRUE) ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE role='admin'); Task 1 (Wave 1) vs Task 9 (Wave 8); server/migrations/migrate.go:29-53
findings.description: The migration hard-creates a row users('ADMIN_LOGIN_2', role='admin', has_access=TRUE) and runs automatically on container start (cmd/main.go:32-34). The spec's only mitigation is manual replacement before rollout plus `grep ADMIN_LOGIN_2 004_access_control.up.sql` in Task 9's Verify-smoke — and Task 9 sits in Wave 8, seven waves after the migration is authored, while dev/CI environments will already have run the file. The mitigation is structurally unable to work: migrate.go records the version in schema_migrations and skips any already-applied file (migrate.go:31-34), and the project has no down migrations. Once the placeholder version has been applied anywhere, editing 004 later does NOT remove the seeded admin row; the acceptance criterion checks the FILE, not the database. Anyone able to authenticate with a Yandex login that collates equal to ADMIN_LOGIN_2 (users.id is VARCHAR(255) under MariaDB's default case- and accent-insensitive collation, migrations/002_costing_schema.up.sql:1-4) immediately holds role='admin' — EnsureUser explicitly preserves role on login (Decision 11), so the login attaches to the pre-seeded admin row instead of creating a fresh user. Hardcoding a live privileged principal into an auto-applied, irreversible artifact is the wrong mechanism regardless of the placeholder.
findings.recommendation: Remove all admin seeding from the migration. Provision admins from configuration read at startup (ADMIN_LOGINS env var — the alternative rejected in Decision 4; reconsider it: it is revocable, environment-scoped and never lands in git) or as a documented one-off SQL executed by the operator after deploy. If the seed must stay in SQL it must (a) contain no placeholder — enforced by a pre-commit/CI grep gate, not a Wave 8 checklist, and (b) be paired with a 005 cleanup migration `DELETE FROM users WHERE id='ADMIN_LOGIN_2'` so an already-applied placeholder is reversible. Add an acceptance criterion asserting against the DATABASE: `SELECT id FROM users WHERE role='admin'` returns exactly the two intended logins.

findings.location: tech-spec.md Decision 8 ("При пустом списке проверка пропускается"); server/internal/handler/cors.go:13-15; docker-compose.yml (app service, no CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS); docker-compose.prod.yml CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS: ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS}; .github/workflows/deploy.yml; server/internal/config/config.go:77
findings.description: RequireSameOrigin is the feature's entire CSRF defence and it is designed to fail OPEN, keyed to a variable that has nothing to do with CSRF. In prod the value is written into $HOME/poshivon/.env as CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS}; an unset GitHub secret expands to empty, envOrDefault returns "", splitCSV returns nil, WithCORS returns `next` unwrapped (cors.go:13-15) and — per Decision 8 — RequireSameOrigin also becomes a no-op. Nothing logs, nothing fails to start, and the application keeps working perfectly, because the SPA and the API are same-origin behind the proxy and never needed CORS in the first place. That is exactly the condition under which an operator would leave the secret empty. The remaining defence is then COOKIE_SAMESITE, itself an unvalidated secret that silently degrades to Lax on a typo (auth.go:513-522) and, if ever set to `none` (a plausible choice for a split-origin dev/staging host), leaves cookie-authenticated POST /api/v1/admin/users/{login}/access reachable from any website: one hidden form submitted by a logged-in admin grants an attacker full product access. Decision 8's own rationale acknowledges Access-Control-Allow-Credentials makes cross-site use expected, then makes the countermeasure optional.
findings.recommendation: Make the check unconditional and self-configuring: when the allowed-origin list is empty, fall back to comparing the Origin's scheme+host against the request's own Host header (same-origin) instead of skipping; keep the list as an ADDITIVE allowlist for the split-origin dev case. Additionally: (1) refuse to start, or log at ERROR, when CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS is empty and COOKIE_SAMESITE=none; (2) validate COOKIE_SAMESITE/COOKIE_SECURE at startup instead of silently defaulting; (3) add an acceptance criterion "с пустым CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS изменяющий запрос с посторонним Origin отклоняется" — the current criterion only exercises the configured case and would pass on a fail-open build.

findings.location: tech-spec.md — Architecture routing table (`/auth/*` — «без изменений»); Decision 9; client/src/pages/AuthCallback.jsx:47-53; server/internal/handler/auth.go:99-168
findings.description: The origin check is scoped to /api/v1/* only, and the OAuth `state` introduced by Decision 9 is generated and verified entirely in the browser (sessionStorage -> AuthCallback). The server endpoint that actually mints sessions, POST /auth/yandex/code, still accepts any `code` from any origin with no state, no PKCE and no origin check. An attacker therefore does not need to defeat the client check — they skip it: a page on evil.com issues fetch('https://poshivon.ru/auth/yandex/code', {method:'POST', credentials:'include', body:'{"code":"<attacker-code>"}'}) and the victim's browser is issued ya_access/ya_refresh cookies bound to the ATTACKER's Yandex identity (login CSRF / session fixation). SameSite does not stop it — SameSite governs cookie sending, not Set-Cookie on the response. The victim then works inside the attacker's account: settings, chats and calculations they enter are written under the attacker's user_id and are readable by the attacker afterwards; if the attacker's account is one of the seeded admins the victim is also silently operating an admin session. POST /auth/logout (forced logout) and POST /auth/refresh are likewise unprotected. Decision 9's stated goal — «чужой код авторизации нельзя подсунуть в сессию пользователя» — is therefore not achieved by a client-side-only state check.
findings.recommendation: Extend RequireSameOrigin to all non-GET/HEAD routes including /auth/* (one line in main.go; the SPA always sends Origin on fetch POSTs), and move `state` server-side: issue it from the server (short-lived HttpOnly SameSite=Lax cookie or a signed value), and have HandleYandexCode require and compare it before calling exchangeCodeWithYandex, rejecting with 400 on mismatch or absence. Keep the sessionStorage check as defence in depth, not as the control. Add acceptance criteria: POST /auth/yandex/code with a foreign Origin -> 403; without a matching state -> 400.

findings.description: The `state` design is underspecified in exactly the places where implementations fail open. The spec says only «генерирует случайный state» — it does not mandate a CSPRNG (an implementer reaching for Math.random().toString(36) produces a guessable value), does not say the stored value is single-use (it must be removed before the exchange, like consumeAuthReturnTo at yandexAuth.js:114-123, otherwise a replayed callback still validates), gives it no expiry, and — most importantly — does not define the branch where sessionStorage holds NO state (new tab, cleared storage, storage exception; the existing helpers swallow storage errors and return null, yandexAuth.js:109/120). Faced with "no stored state", an implementer optimising for not breaking login writes `if (storedState && storedState !== param) fail`, which reduces the check to nothing.
findings.recommendation: Specify in Decision 9: state = crypto.randomUUID() or crypto.getRandomValues(32 bytes) hex; stored under a dedicated key; read-and-delete before the exchange; absence of a stored state, absence of the callback parameter, or any mismatch aborts the login and never falls through to exchangeYandexCode. Add a Verify-user step: opening the callback URL in a fresh tab (no sessionStorage) must NOT complete a login.

findings.location: tech-spec.md — whole document; Phase 1 tasks 1-15 and Phase 2 tasks 16-20
findings.description: The feature introduces a privilege model and contains no security logging requirement whatsoever. Nothing in either phase logs successful/failed authentication, session identity rejections (session_identity_missing), 401/403 denials, RequireAdmin denials, or — most seriously — grant and revoke of access. The only audit surface is decided_by/decided_at on access_requests, which (a) covers only grants routed through a request and says nothing about a SetAccess call on a user who never filed one (the spec does not define what DecideRequest does when no row exists), (b) is overwritten by the next decision, and (c) is destroyed by ON DELETE CASCADE when the user row goes away. After an incident there is no way to answer "who granted this account access and when, and who revoked it". This is not a Phase-2 deferral — it is absent from both phases; the Phase 2 SMTP notification is an alerting channel, not an audit trail, so shipping Phase 1 without it leaves privilege changes both unlogged and unnotified.
findings.recommendation: Add to Task 4/Task 5 structured log lines (stdout is already the sink) for auth_failed{reason}, access_denied{login,path,reason}, admin_action{actor,target,granted}, session_identity_missing. Add an append-only access_audit(actor, target, action, at) table to migration 004 written in the same transaction as SetAccess, and make it the source of truth for "who granted" instead of decided_by. Add an acceptance criterion that a grant and a revoke each produce an audit row naming the acting admin.

findings.description: Decision 17 fixes only the `default` branch. Five of the six branches in writeAPIDomainError still return err.Error() verbatim: ErrInvalidArgument -> 400, ErrNotFound -> 404, and the three substring-matched branches (rate_limit_exceeded -> 429, service_unavailable -> 503, timeout -> 504). Repository errors are wrapped with operation context and identifiers (fmt.Errorf("query settings: %w", err) postgres.go:187, "upsert user settings" :188, fmt.Errorf("chat %q not found: %w", ...)), and any driver error whose text contains the word "timeout" (MySQL `context deadline exceeded`, `i/o timeout`, `Lock wait timeout exceeded`) is routed to the 504 branch and echoed to the client with the underlying driver/schema text. DeepSeek errors reaching 503/504 can carry the upstream endpoint. The claim in Decision 17 that this «закрывает и существующие маршруты» is true for one branch only. Substring matching on error text is also a fragile classifier.
findings.recommendation: Return fixed client-facing text on every branch that is not a deliberate, validated 400 message, and log the wrapped error server-side in all cases. Replace the three strings.Contains branches with sentinel errors (service.ErrRateLimited, ErrUpstreamUnavailable, ErrUpstreamTimeout) returned by the DeepSeek client. Add an acceptance criterion covering a 404/504 path, not only the 500 path — the current criterion «Ответ 500 не содержит текста внутренней ошибки» would pass while 504 still leaks.

findings.location: tech-spec.md — Data Models (seed uses 'RoGogDBD'), Decision 11 (EnsureUser); server/migrations/002_costing_schema.up.sql:1-4 (users.id VARCHAR(255), default collation)
findings.description: The whole authorization model keys on users.id = the Yandex login, but the spec never fixes a normalization rule, and it seeds mixed case ('RoGogDBD') while Yandex returns the login lowercased from https://login.yandex.ru/info. Whether the seeded admin and the real login are the same row depends entirely on the table collation — MariaDB 11.4's default for VARCHAR is case- AND accent-insensitive. Two failure modes, both bad: (a) if the column is ever created/altered with a binary or case-sensitive collation, EnsureUser inserts a SECOND row `rogogdbd` with role='user', the seeded admin row is inert, and there is no admin at all — the feature bricks itself, and since only admins can grant access nobody can be granted access without manual SQL; (b) under the accent-insensitive default, identities differing only by case/diacritics collapse to one authorization subject, which is the wrong property for a security key and is what makes the ADMIN_LOGIN_2 placeholder reachable by e.g. admin_login_2.
findings.recommendation: Normalize explicitly rather than relying on collation: lowercase/trim the login in EnsureUser, in the middleware identity, in the admin {login} path segment and in the migration seed, and state the rule in Decision 11. Declare the collation explicitly in migration 004 (ALTER TABLE users MODIFY id VARCHAR(255) COLLATE utf8mb4_bin) once values are normalized, so the key is exact-match. Add a contract test: EnsureUser('RoGogDBD') and EnsureUser('rogogdbd') resolve to one row that keeps role='admin'.

findings.location: server/internal/handler/auth.go:121-128 (HandleYandexCode); tech-spec.md Decision 7 / Solution §4 («Закрытие путей обхода входа»)
findings.description: The spec declares the login-bypass surface closed, but HandleYandexCode still takes `redirect_uri` from the request body and only falls back to cfg.YandexRedirectURI when absent, then forwards it to Yandex's token endpoint. The value is fully caller-controlled and is part of the code-exchange binding; the server never checks it against its own configuration. Exploitation is bounded by Yandex rejecting unregistered redirect URIs, but it means the server exchanges codes minted for a redirect target it did not choose, and it widens the attack surface of the one endpoint that mints sessions (composes with the login-CSRF finding above). Decision 7 rejected keeping /auth/yandex precisely to avoid «неиспользуемую поверхность атаки»; the same reasoning applies here.
findings.recommendation: Ignore redirect_uri from the body and always use cfg.YandexRedirectURI; if the body value must be accepted for the dev flow, compare it for exact equality with the configured value and reject with 400 otherwise. Drop the parameter from exchangeYandexCode's client signature (yandexAuth.js:81-102). Add it to Task 4's scope with an acceptance criterion.

findings.location: tech-spec.md Decision 10, Decision 4, API contract table
findings.description: There is no de-provisioning path for the admin role. Decision 10 makes has_access irrelevant for admins and the UI checkbox uncheckable for them; the API exposes no way to change `role`; role is only writable by a migration that has already run. Consequence: a compromised, departing or mistakenly-seeded admin account cannot be revoked through the product at all — the only remedy is manual `docker exec ... mariadb` SQL on prod under incident pressure, with no runbook in the spec. Combined with the ADMIN_LOGIN_2 finding, the system can ship with an admin nobody can remove without direct DB access. Decision 10's rationale (protect against self-lockout) is sound, but self-lockout protection and irrevocability are not the same requirement.
findings.recommendation: Keep the self-lockout guard but add a revocation path: allow an admin to demote another admin (never themselves) via the existing admin endpoint, with a server-side invariant that at least one admin must remain, enforced in the same transaction. At minimum, document the exact SQL revocation runbook in the deploy task and add it to the Risks table with the incident scenario, rather than leaving revocation undefined.

findings.description: Every security-relevant configuration knob in this service fails open silently, and the feature adds a fourth one that inherits the pattern instead of fixing it. COOKIE_SECURE defaults to FALSE (config.go:68) and envBool returns the fallback on any unparsable value — an unset or misspelled secret means the ya_access cookie, which carries the raw Yandex OAuth token, is sent over plaintext HTTP. COOKIE_SAMESITE falls back to Lax on any unrecognised value (auth.go:519-521) with no warning. CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS empty disables both CORS and (per Decision 8) the origin check. None are validated at startup, none are asserted by an acceptance criterion, and config.Load() cannot even return an error today (it always returns nil). The feature raises the stakes on all of them because the same cookies now confer role='admin'.
findings.recommendation: Add a validation pass in config.Load() that returns an error (main.go already log.Fatalf's on it) when the deployment is not local: COOKIE_SECURE must be true, COOKIE_SAMESITE must parse to a recognised value (reject unknown strings instead of defaulting), CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS must be non-empty when COOKIE_SAMESITE=none. Gate relaxed behaviour behind an explicit APP_ENV=dev rather than behind the absence of configuration. Add a post-deploy check asserting Set-Cookie on prod carries Secure, HttpOnly and the expected SameSite.

findings.location: tech-spec.md — Data Models (access_requests.message VARCHAR(1000)), API contract (POST /api/v1/access/requests), Decision 14, Task 16 (Phase 2 SMTPNotifier)
findings.description: access_requests.message is user-supplied, but the API contract table documents no request body for POST /api/v1/access/requests and no validation of length or content is specified anywhere — a message longer than 1000 chars becomes a MariaDB 1406 error surfaced as a 500. More importantly, that value plus externally-sourced display_name and email (stored per Decision 12, shown to admins) flow into the Phase 2 email built by hand with net/smtp. Decision 14 mentions RFC 2047 encoding only for the fixed Cyrillic SUBJECT and net/mail validation only for addresses read from CONFIGURATION — nothing covers user-controlled values placed into the message. Any CR/LF in an interpolated value at header position yields SMTP header injection (arbitrary Bcc/Reply-To, mail forged from the product's domain); the same values are rendered in the admin list, where safety depends on nobody reaching for dangerouslySetInnerHTML.
findings.recommendation: Define the request body in the API contract; validate `message` server-side (max 1000 runes, strip control characters, reject CR/LF) in AccessService.CreateRequest and return ErrInvalidArgument -> 400 instead of letting the DB fail. In Task 16 state that every interpolated value goes in the BODY only, never in a header, that all values are stripped of CR/LF before use, and that recipients come exclusively from ADMIN_NOTIFY_EMAILS validated with net/mail. Add a notifier test: a login/message containing \r\n produces no additional header.

findings.location: server/internal/handler/metrics.go:23-45; server/cmd/main.go:76-78; tech-spec.md Risks table (last row) and API contract (POST /api/v1/admin/users/{login}/access)
findings.description: The Risks table dismisses the metrics-label issue with «оставшийся {login} в админском маршруте доступен только администраторам» — that is wrong about how the middleware is layered. WithMetrics wraps the whole mux OUTSIDE any authorization (main.go:76-78), so the label is recorded for every request including 401s and 403s. looksLikeID (metrics.go:35-45) only collapses pure integers and strings longer than 8 chars containing a hyphen, so any unauthenticated caller can mint unbounded distinct `path` label values with POST /api/v1/admin/users/<random>/access — a memory-exhaustion / cardinality-explosion vector against the app process and Prometheus, reachable with no credentials. Real logins of legitimate users also land in metrics, scraped into Grafana and retained 15 days (a data-minimisation issue for a login + access-status pair).
findings.recommendation: Normalize by ROUTE, not by heuristic: match the path against the known route templates and emit the template (/api/v1/admin/users/:login/access), falling back to a single `other` bucket for unmatched paths. Correct the Risks table entry — the current mitigation text is factually incorrect and would let this ship. Keep /metrics denied at the proxy (it already is in deploy.yml) and bind it away from the public port in dev too.

findings.location: tech-spec.md — Architecture routing table; server/cmd/main.go:39-78; Task 5
findings.description: Ordering inside each chain is fail-closed (RequireSameOrigin -> RequireAuth -> RequireAccess/RequireAdmin is the right sequence, and Go's ServeMux cleans paths before matching so no ..//  bypass exists). The weakness is at the registration level: protection is an ALLOWLIST of three prefixes, so any future handler registered under /api/v1/ — or a typo'd prefix — is silently unguarded, and nothing in the spec or the tests would catch it. Two behaviours are also left undefined: what the middleware does when GetUser returns ErrNotFound (valid session, users row missing/deleted) and what it does when the repository returns a transport error (DB down). Both must terminate the request; an implementer writing `if err != nil && !errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) { 500 }` and falling through is a plausible mistake.
findings.recommendation: Register a default-deny catch-all mux.Handle("/api/v1/", <401/403 handler>) after the three specific prefixes so an unmatched API path is denied rather than accidentally 404'd, and add an integration test asserting that an unregistered /api/v1/* path is not served without authentication. State explicitly in Decision 6 that any error from GetUser (including ErrNotFound) results in 403/500 and never proceeds to the wrapped handler; add a middleware test with a failing repository stub.

findings.location: tech-spec.md — API contract; server/internal/handler/auth.go (all /auth routes); AccessService.ListUsers
findings.description: No rate limiting anywhere, before or after this feature. /auth/yandex/code and /auth/refresh are unauthenticated and each triggers an outbound HTTPS round-trip to Yandex (10s client timeout, auth.go:36-38), so they are a cheap amplification/exhaustion target. RequireAuth performs a DB lookup keyed on a SHA-256 of an attacker-supplied cookie on every request. EnsureUser means any person on the internet with any Yandex account can create a users row simply by logging in, then one access_requests row — the admin list (GET /api/v1/admin/users, unpaginated, returns every user with email) degrades under that noise and there is no way to purge it. The PRIMARY KEY bounds requests to one per account, which is the only limiter present.
findings.recommendation: Add a per-IP token bucket in front of /auth/* and /api/v1/access/requests (a small in-process limiter needs no new dependency, consistent with the project's zero-dependency policy). Paginate or cap ListUsers and give the admin list a filter by request status so a flood of empty accounts cannot hide real requests. Provide a way to delete a user row (ON DELETE CASCADE is already in place on access_requests).

findings.location: server/internal/auth/store.go:11-21, 36-66; server/internal/handler/auth.go:387-393, 447-449; tech-spec.md Risks table (accepted risk) and Decision 12
findings.description: Reported for completeness because the spec accepts this risk while simultaneously increasing its cost. The raw Yandex access token is stored in plaintext in oauth_sessions.yandex_access_token, the Yandex refresh token in plaintext in yandex_refresh_token, and the access token is ALSO mirrored into the client's ya_access cookie and compared with a non-constant-time != (auth.go:447). Decision 12 widens the token scope to login:email, so a DB read or cookie disclosure now yields a broader-privileged upstream credential, and after this feature the same cookie pair also confers role='admin'. The Risks table states this correctly and defers it; the deferral is defensible because the fix is a real refactor, not because the risk is small.
findings.recommendation: Bound the deferral: stop mirroring the upstream token into a cookie (validateSession already looks the session up by refresh hash, so the access cookie is redundant — issue an opaque id instead), and encrypt yandex_refresh_token at rest. Both are far smaller than the full decoupling the Risks row describes. Meanwhile use subtle.ConstantTimeCompare at auth.go:447 and make COOKIE_SECURE non-negotiable in prod (see the config finding).

findings.description: The dev compose hardcodes MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD=root and poshivon/poshivon and publishes 3306 on the host with no bind address, so it listens on all interfaces of the developer machine. Pre-existing, but this feature makes that database the store of role and has_access: anyone reaching the port (shared network, WSL host, VM) can self-grant admin with one UPDATE, and the same compose is what the AVP tells the agent to run. The dev compose also lacks CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS and COOKIE_SAMESITE entirely, which is precisely the fail-open configuration described above — meaning every developer run and every AVP run exercises a build with CSRF protection disabled, so the control is never actually observed working.
findings.recommendation: Bind the published port to 127.0.0.1 ("127.0.0.1:3306:3306") and read dev credentials from a gitignored .env with non-default values. Add CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173,http://localhost:8080 and COOKIE_SAMESITE=Lax to the dev compose so the origin check is exercised in dev and in the AVP rather than skipped.

findings.location: /home/makar/PoshivOn/.gitignore (last line); server/internal/config/config.go:43-48; tech-spec.md Risks table («SMTP-креды утекают в репозиторий — pre-commit хуков и gitleaks в проекте нет»); Tasks 16/19
findings.description: I scanned the tracked tree for hardcoded credentials (API_KEY/SECRET/PASSWORD/TOKEN assignments, connection strings, private keys, base64 blobs) across .go/.js/.jsx/.yml/.sql/.json and found none tracked — that part is clean, and git ls-files shows no .env committed. The gap is preventive: .gitignore ignores exactly `.env` and nothing else, so .env.local, .env.prod and server/.env are all committable, while config.go:43-48 actively searches four .env paths and thereby invites per-directory files. The project has no gitleaks/pre-commit gate, and the spec mitigates its own named risk with a prose instruction in a task description. Phase 2 introduces SMTP_PASSWORD — the first credential a developer will be tempted to try locally.
findings.recommendation: Broaden .gitignore to `.env`, `.env.*`, `*.env`, `!.env.example`, and add the gitleaks pre-commit hook the infrastructure-setup skill already provides — one config file that converts a prose risk into an enforced gate before Phase 2 lands. Ship an .env.example with empty SMTP values so nobody edits a real one in-tree.
